content: That's pretty cool, but it means the sorry habit will remain

This is getting off topic for this, but I am curious what makes people put sorry in the proof that they are actively working at (with the parse error gone). I feel like that’s just a workaround for some UX deficiency that people don’t just write their proofs linearly. When programming, you don’t put exit in your python script as you are writing!
2 messages were moved here from #lean4 > Test users for try-on-empty-by by Joachim Breitner.

I guess, it could be to keep track of where I have unfinished goals? Since the "unsolved goals" error pops up at the beginning of the tactic block, but the part I am working on is at the end, there is no marker at the end to show which part needs working on, so I put a sorry there.

Joachim Breitner said:

When programming, you don’t put exit in your python script as you are writing!

idk about you but I always start my functions with

def foo():
    pass

to avoid the parse error

Ok, I understand that you want to mark unfinished goals that you are not actively working on, if you set them aside for now. But for the theorem you are presently staring at, after

theorem foo : Bar := by

what itches you to write sorry there instead of just typing ahead with your proof?
The presence of an error

Snir Broshi schrieb:

to avoid the parse error

Right, I understand that, but the parse error is gone.

Also, it could be to suppress the "unsolved goals" error, since normally if I have an error it means something is wrong (type mismatch, or failed to synthesize instance, or simp failed to make progress), but the "unsolved goals" error is expected.

I agree that no more parse error is a nice win, but there's still a blatant error in my text editor screaming at me.
The distinction between error types is irrelevant there.
See also #new members > `calc` syntax error @ 💬 for a similar habit about calc that exists because of Lean errors.

Hmm, ok. At some point I was wondering whether the UI should differentiate between more clearly “you did something wrong” and “you did not do all of it yet”. At some point I mused whether every prefix of a correct proof should not be annotated in any way.

I get the sense that if we had that, people might not reach for these work-arounds. But there were other problems making that hard.

Joachim Breitner said:

Ok, I understand that you want to mark unfinished goals that you are not actively working on, if you set them aside for now. But for the theorem you are presently staring at, after

theorem foo : Bar := by

what itches you to write sorry there instead of just typing ahead with your proof?

For me it's that I'm in the habit now wanting my cursor to be at the start of a line before looking at the infoview (e.g., rwa is an example of a tactic that doesn't give the right infoview if you put your cursor at the end of the line).
So you press Enter-Space-Space, right – but why sorry? Or are you saying that after some tactics that does not give you the right goal state? That sounds like a bug to me.

Maybe it's just that it feels strange to have the cursor floating in the void indented two spaces with no other text? But also the sorry provides nice closure (as people mentioned before, often when you're working on a long proof, you might have several sorries scattered throughout, so you get in the habit of wanting every goal to be proved or sorried, because I think unsorried goals can cause problems later in the proof?).
Hmm, unsorried goals should behave like sorried goals in later parts of the proof (At least with the parser fix.)

I am also guilty of the sorry habit. The reason is that Lean gives the error "unsolved goals", I don't like seeing errors on my screen because, so I type sorry to make the error disappear, and I write my proof above this sorry.

I guess the real usability reason of doing this, is that this "unsolved goals" error is noise, and by ending the proof by sorry it means that now every error showing on my screen is now a legitimate error that needs my attention immediately. On the other hand, this "unsolved goals" error is useful in proof maintenance, e.g. if I change some definition and now the last tactic does not close the goal.
Thanks, that’s a good, concise explanation! I agree that errors that are (in your current workflow) just noise are a good reason to silence them by whatever means that are not more inconvenient.

Since we are discussing the topic, something else I am guilty for, because of the same reasons:

When I use a tactic that creates multiple goals (e.g. split, induction, etc), I start by writing

· sorry
· sorry
· sorry
· sorry
-- ...

(I could also write all_goals sorry and accomplish the same thing)

Joachim Breitner said:

So you press Enter-Space-Space, right – but why sorry? Or are you saying that after some tactics that does not give you the right goal state? That sounds like a bug to me.

I have the habit of saving the file every time I finish typing and want to think. If I press Enter-Space-Space-Ctrl-s my cursor returns to the start of the line because the whitespace gets trimmed on saving.

Joachim Breitner said:

When programming, you don’t put exit in your python script as you are writing!

I definitely tend to fill this out with the default return ... at the bottom before starting to write the body to get rid of the error

Of course with regular programming it's easier to 'fill this hole correctly' as you have an idea of what the function should return by default, but the trigger is still the error and I expect I might change the value later as I structure the function.

Just curious, why is this considered such a sin if the sorries are so blatant anyways? On my example above, I would never expect the IDE to 'compensate' for me and not show me that error: I want to know that I have 'places where I need to fill out a return'. With linted sorries it's even better because I know that I won't just forget and leave it that way.

It's not a sin! I'm just curious and want to understand how users use Lean. And also I believe that ideally you would not have to write things that you then have to remove, in that sense it's a symptom of an insufficient UI. But not a sin on your side! :-)
haha sorry, sin might be too strong a word, but the attitude in the chat was about being 'guilty' of it :-)
That wasn't my intention!

As one more data point, writing sorry for a goal I plan to return to later is such an ingrained habit that it took me a moment to even understand the premise of this thread! To me it just feels natural as a syntactic placeholder.
Right, I use sorry to “not now, will do later” as well. I'm interested here in the case of the proof you are actually working on, though.

Something similar: I occasionally find myself writing

· skip

such that the big error line for the unsolved goals is localized to the skip instead of whatever big tactic I want to put there
Do we still have the big confusing error line? I thought we fixed that one
Looks like we still have this. I misremembered.

Ah, we decided that we want to fix it, but didn't yet :-)
https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/issues/8919

FWIW not only do I write sorry immediately after stating a theorem (and even have a VSCode snippet

    "Sorry": {
        "prefix": "sorry",
        "body": [
            "· $0",
            "  sorry",
            "· ",
            "  sorry"
        ],
        "description": "Two goals suddenly? Change one `sorry` to two"
    }

for when a tactic creates a second goal), but I encourage all my undergraduates to do the same thing. I have noticed that if you let beginner mathematicians become complacent about having errors in their script as they are coding, then you end up with them having errors all over their file.

Théophile Wallez said:

(I could also write all_goals sorry and accomplish the same thing)

As a fun fact, the stop tactic is the same as repeat sorry, but its parses a bit differently: it actually takes in a tactic sequence as input and effectively comments it out. This means that stop by itself doesn't work; if you want to use stop by itself you have to write stop done or stop skip or stop {}. It's unclear if this is intentional, as the documentation for stop doesn't seem to mention this.

Here, as long as let x : Nat := "hi" parses, stop effectively comments it out so you don't get type errors.

example : True := by
  stop
  let x : Nat := "hi"
Sounds like something we should fix. And I keep forgetting the name of that tactic, when I need that feature :sweat_smile:, thanks for reminding me!

I find the fact that it comments out the following tactics really useful, though: when I'm working on a slow proof, it is very convenient to stub out parts by just writing stop before the various branches.
Yes, absolutely, that's the whole point, isn't it?

Unfortunately stop interacts wrongly with the unused variable linter: the linter correctly ignores any declaration containing sorry (because the variable might become used once the sorry is filled in), but doesn't ignore declarations containing stop.

Joachim Breitner said:

Right, I understand that, but the parse error is gone.

Since when?
This is on latest Mathlib in the web editor

Those are 2 parse errors, right?
Also, every line between the two theorems gets red squiggles.
Oh, it's gone on the latest Lean nightly. I think I'll probably change habits if there's no parse error anymore on an empty by-block.

I can just add to what's been mentioned in various forms here: UI-wise I always want to be in a state with no red errors because that gives me confidence that Lean is still able to parse everything written. As soon that there is some red error somewhere, there is some risk that there might be other subsequent errors which might not be displayed correctly due to parsing going wild. This confidence is usually worth the effort to write sorry (or, I like mathlib's done)

I haven't fully thought about whether it would solve the problem to make "unsolved goals" a "warning" which behaves exactly like the "uses sorry" warning, but I think it might.

In NNG we always had to treat the "unsolved goals" error manually because it's the only error which isn't really an error but it's just always there as long as there is work to do. This might be another indication that it should be something else instead of an error. But there might also be compelling reasons to leave it as error, I didnt spent much time thinking about it.

Perhaps one could special-case the highlighting for that specific error in the VSCode extension?

Then it gets to remain an error (since it really is an unfinished definition which cannot compile. We're spoiled by Lean nevertheless almost always managing to compile subsequent definitions). I also think it's convenient to have it as an error in the output of e.g. lake build, just not while writing a proof.

It’s good to brainstorm usability and share your experiences and habits, but let’s not jump to half-baked implementation ideas, that's not the path to a good UX design.

So to manage expectations: Nothing in this thread is supposed to be understood as an explicit or implicit promise that anything here will change or will not change :-)

It could be much more meaningful to e.g. always provide implicit sorry for each WIP theorem and result in a warning "theorem uses sorry statement" instead of the error that forces more people to always write "sorry" (I actually prefer "admit" here which is more formal). After all an unfinished theorem is the same as WIP theorem being typed and both have the problem of not being complete and equipped with a proof, all while saving us from constantly writing sorries just for the sake of developing a statement or a proof.

How is it an issue whatsoever, as long as you have it removed when you are done?

If I have some kind of wrapper proof and I understand what the outer skeleton needs to do, I can put admit into an internal compartment so that I can get a clear outer structure to compile. Then I can go back into the compartment(s) and replace the admit with the required mechanisms. Sure you could do it linearly, maybe its more effort maybe not, depends on how you hold shapes in your head. Either way you will end up not having a "sorry" in your proof at the end.

In other languages, I would just comment out sections or if forced to, pass some fake value (actually dangerous if you don't keep track of it!). I like the lean sorry system because I am not tempted to do anything dangerous, it gives you a great big yellow triangle linter and its going to show up in the #print statement at the end if you somehow manage to forget to deal with the lemma linter... which for me is never but hey, it's there.

Guard rails on elevated platforms are great, even if you never lean on them.

Jon Eugster said:

I can just add to what's been mentioned in various forms here: UI-wise I always want to be in a state with no red errors because that gives me confidence that Lean is still able to parse everything written. As soon that there is some red error somewhere, there is some risk that there might be other subsequent errors which might not be displayed correctly due to parsing going wild. This confidence is usually worth the effort to write sorry (or, I like mathlib's done)

I haven't fully thought about whether it would solve the problem to make "unsolved goals" a "warning" which behaves exactly like the "uses sorry" warning, but I think it might.

In NNG we always had to treat the "unsolved goals" error manually because it's the only error which isn't really an error but it's just always there as long as there is work to do. This might be another indication that it should be something else instead of an error. But there might also be compelling reasons to leave it as error, I didnt spent much time thinking about it.

This is exactly what I do. Write a lemma, deal with any red errors as I go until it is clear, then check every linter and only proceed if they are acceptable. Don't start a new lemma until that one is "done" in this manner. It seems very reassuring to proceed in this manner, and I never have build errors.

Joachim Breitner said:

When programming, you don’t put exit in your python script as you are writing!

Of course you put todo!()s in your code when you write it.
And Smalltalk has Object>>notYetImplemented for the very same purpose.
It's a common feature in good programming languages (so not in Python it seems...).

Joachim Breitner said:

Ok, I understand that you want to mark unfinished goals that you are not actively working on, if you set them aside for now. But for the theorem you are presently staring at, after

theorem foo : Bar := by

what itches you to write sorry there instead of just typing ahead with your proof?

Yeah, that one is because of an annoying error. Replacing that error with automatic sorry would be an improvement I think.

I don't think repeat sorry is a good idea here though, I believe Lean should instead nudge you towards structured proofs.
Considering Joachim literally quoted the Python feature which does it, and the point is "no one uses that while programming" not "this doesn't exist", that's a slightly weird potshot.

Plamen Dimitrov said:

It could be much more meaningful to e.g. always provide implicit sorry for each WIP theorem and result in a warning "theorem uses sorry statement" instead of the error that forces more people to always write "sorry" (I actually prefer "admit" here which is more formal). After all an unfinished theorem is the same as WIP theorem being typed and both have the problem of not being complete and equipped with a proof, all while saving us from constantly writing sorries just for the sake of developing a statement or a proof.

Another case to support this point - if there is an actual error in the syntax or some type checking this will sometimes overlap with the error about missing proof (which should technically be the same as the warning for a missing proof if we just allow for one default implicit sorry in the end) and hide it or overlay on top of it. I think what I describe here is hopefully impartial and simple equivalent - the behavior

-- warns that theorem is not proven!
theorem t (h: a = 2) (h' : a = b) : b = 2 := by
  rw [h'] at h
  sorry

could be easily made equivalent to

-- could simply warn by adding implicit sorry in the end if it was implemented feature
theorem t (h: a = 2) (h' : a = b) : b = 2 := by
  rw [h'] at h
  -- sorry is already assumed here

which would not hide any actual errors instead of forcing people to manually type sorry for e.g. a split of 10 cases for a proof.

How is it an issue whatsoever, as long as you have it removed when you are done?

It saves boilerplate. Of course I understand your point about seeing the structure of the proof early, my worry with this however is that you are never sure this is the correct proof structure for real until you are done. This then reduces to my previous points.
